idiom_name: opaque builder struct: cfg_builder_new / chainable cfg_builder_* setters / cfg_builder_build
implementation_notes: C has no constructors, default arguments or exceptions, so the builder is written by hand: declare an incomplete type in the public header (typedef struct cfg_builder cfg_builder;), export cfg_builder_new/cfg_builder_free, one setter per optional field that returns the builder pointer so calls can be chained, and a terminal cfg_builder_build that validates the accumulated values and returns a const product. The GoF Director becomes a plain function applying a fixed sequence of setters (cfg_default_client(cfg_builder *b)), and the ConcreteBuilder role exists only when the product has several representations. Use the builder when values arrive from several sources or cross-field rules must hold; for a handful of fields a designated initializer (struct cfg c = { .timeout_ms = 5000 };) is simpler and needs no allocation.
pitfalls: Ownership is by convention only: the builder and the product need separate release functions (cfg_builder_free vs cfg_free), and a setter that returns the builder by value makes chained calls mutate a temporary copy.

Nothing checks required fields or step order: every setter must install a documented default and build must re-check the required values (NULL/sentinel) itself, or the failure turns into a crash inside the product.
The return value is already used for chaining, so a failing step has no channel: store the error in the builder (b->error) or report it through build returning NULL plus an out-parameter.
